title: Reactivity series
learningObjective: Understand how metals can be arranged in a reactivity series based on their reactions with: water; dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid; Understand how metals can be arranged in a reactivity series based on their displacement reactions between: metals and metal oxides; metals and aqueous solutions of metal salts; Know the order of reactivity of these metals: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold; Know the conditions under which iron rusts; Understand how the rusting of iron may be prevented by: barrier methods; galvanising; sacrificial protection; Understand the terms: oxidation; reduction; redox; oxidising agent; reducing agent in terms of gain or loss of oxygen and loss or gain of electrons; Practical: Investigate reactions between dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids and metals (e.g. magnesium, zinc and iron)

sections.title: Reactivity Series
sections.markdown:
Not all metals are equally worth their salt when it comes to reacting.
Drop a lump of potassium into water and it skates about furiously,
bursting into flame; leave a gold ring in the sea for a thousand years
and it comes out unchanged. Chemists capture that contrast in a single
ranked list — the **[[reactivity-series]]** — and this chapter builds
it, uses it and then explains the reactions that hold it together. The
series does more than rank metals: it introduces the idea of a
**[[redox-reaction]]**, in which one substance takes oxygen (or
electrons) and another gives it up, and it powers one of the most
useful reaction types in chemistry, the **[[displacement-reaction]]**,
where a more reactive metal steals a less reactive metal's place in a
compound.

The payoff for learning the series is enormous, and it is not abstract.
When aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide, the reaction produces
molten iron hot enough to weld railway rails together on site — a
displacement reaction doing industrial work. When zinc is bolted onto a
ship's steel hull, the zinc corrodes so the iron does not — the series
predicting which metal sacrifices itself. Gold stays bright forever
precisely because it sits at the very bottom of the series: in contact
with air or water it stays chemically unchanged, essentially forever.

Here is the route through the chapter. First you will learn how
reactions with water and with dilute acids arrange metals in the series
and how displacement reactions — with metal oxides and with salt
solutions — refine the ordering, meeting oxidation, reduction and the
agent vocabulary on the way. Then comes the order itself, learned
straight, followed by the two flagship applications: why iron rusts and
how rusting is beaten with barriers, galvanising and sacrificial
protection. A listed practical ties the whole idea down: investigating
reactions between dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids and metals
such as magnesium, zinc and iron.

:::prior-knowledge
Four earlier chapters load this one. From Chapter 7 (u1:c07) you need
ionic charges and formula-writing — you will deduce formulae like
manganese(II) sulfate from ion charges, exactly as that chapter taught.
From Chapter 9 (u1:c09) you need metallic structure: metal atoms in a
lattice with delocalised electrons, because the electron-transfer view
of redox depends on it. From Chapter 10 (u1:c10) you need ionic
half-equations, which return here as the bookkeeping of oxidation and
reduction. From Chapter 11 (u2:c11) you already know how violently
potassium, sodium and lithium treat cold water — this chapter turns
that memory into a ranking tool. Equations throughout assume the
balancing and state-symbol skills of Chapter 5 (u1:c05).
:::

:::exam-hint
Every objective in this chapter can be examined in Paper 1C as well as
Paper 2C — nothing here is chemistry-only. The most common question
shapes are: arrange metals in order from reaction observations; predict
whether a displacement happens and write the equation; identify the
oxidised and reduced substances and name the agents; and explain rust
prevention in terms of keeping oxygen and water away or supplying a
more reactive metal. Each shape gets its own coaching as the chapter
goes.
:::

:::misconception
"Carbon and hydrogen are metals, because they appear in the reactivity
series." They are not metals — they sit in the series because they are
useful reference points: carbon earns its place through extraction
chemistry and hydrogen through the water and acid reactions that split
the series in two. An examiner who asks "why are carbon and hydrogen
included even though they are non-metals" wants exactly that answer,
not a re-classification of the two elements.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15 orientation items. Before moving on, say
in one sentence what the reactivity series is and in one more what a
displacement reaction is. If both sentences come out cleanly, the
chapter's machinery is ready to build.
:::

sections.title: The Reaction between Magnesium and Copper(ii) Oxide
sections.markdown:
The chapter's model reaction is a fight over oxygen. Mix magnesium
powder with copper(II) oxide and heat the mixture strongly, and the
magnesium tears the oxygen away from the copper: white magnesium oxide
is left behind, and copper metal is set free. Reactions between metals
and metal oxides like this are often called **competition reactions** —
a [[competition-reaction]] pits the two metals against each other for
the oxygen, and the winner is the more
reactive metal. Since magnesium wins, magnesium must sit above copper
in the **[[reactivity-series]]**; that single observation is one rung of
the ladder that the whole chapter assembles.

The same experiment template comes in three versions, and the print
headings announce them: magnesium with copper(II) oxide, magnesium with
zinc oxide, and carbon with copper(II) oxide. Each is a matchup you can
call in advance once you know the ladder. The ladder itself is worth
meeting in full now: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium,
aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold, from
most reactive down to least. Although carbon and hydrogen are not
metals, they are usually included in the series, and this chapter shows
you why — carbon because it decides which ores can be cheaply reduced,
hydrogen because the water and acid reactions later in the chapter use
it as the dividing line.

The safety story for the model reaction is real chemistry: the tube
gets very hot and stays hot long after heating stops, so eye protection
goes on before the mixture is warmed and stays on while the tube cools.
The full demonstration — including why it is done behind screens — is
the next section's business.

:::safety
Wear eye protection throughout. The reaction tube will get very hot and
will remain so for some time — treat the tube as hot long after the
flame is off.
:::

:::exam-hint
When an examiner asks "how can this reaction show that magnesium is
more reactive than copper", the marking points are always the same
three: name the reaction type (displacement/competition), state who
takes the oxygen (magnesium takes oxygen from copper(II) oxide), and
conclude the ranking (so magnesium is above copper in the reactivity
series). Practise writing all three as one linked sentence.
:::

:::misconception
"Heating a mixture hard enough can force any metal to displace any
other." Heat supplies activation energy; it does not rewrite the
reactivity order. Heat copper with magnesium oxide for as long as you
like and nothing happens — copper is below magnesium and cannot take
oxygen from it. The ladder decides the outcome before the burner is
even lit; all the heating does is let the winning metal demonstrate it.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.16/2.17 items. Before moving on, recite the
reactivity series from memory, including carbon and hydrogen in their
correct places, and name the reaction type used to build it. The rest
of the chapter assumes both are automatic.
:::

sections.title: Displacement Reactions Involving Metal Oxides
sections.markdown:
One gram of magnesium powder mixed with one gram of copper(II) oxide,
heated very strongly in a metal bottle cap: usually nothing seems to
happen for a few seconds, and then the mixture erupts in a burst of
sparks and a bright flash of light. Afterwards, traces of white
magnesium oxide are left on the ceramic paper inside. The demonstration
is dramatic precisely because the chemistry is decisive — magnesium is
far above copper, so once the mixture reaches the temperature where the
reaction can start, it races.

This is the defining example of a **[[displacement-reaction]]**: the
less reactive metal, copper, has been displaced from its compound by
the more reactive magnesium. The rule that generalises it is the workhorse
of this chapter — any metal higher in the reactivity series will
displace one lower down from its compound. The rule also cuts the other
way, and the negative case is just as informative: heat copper with
magnesium oxide and nothing happens, because copper cannot prise oxygen
away from a metal above it.

The same rule plays out in the other two matchups. Heating magnesium
with zinc oxide produces zinc metal — magnesium is above zinc, so the
oxygen changes hands:

Mg(s) + ZnO(s) → MgO(s) + Zn(s)

And a black mixture of carbon and copper(II) oxide, heated in a
test-tube, glows red hot with the heat given out by the reaction and
leaves pink-brown copper in the tube. Carbon is above copper in the
reactivity series, so it displaces copper from the oxide:

2CuO(s) + C(s) → 2Cu(s) + CO₂(g)

Carbon's place in the series is not a technicality — it is one of the
most economically important facts in metallurgy. Carbon is included in
the reactivity series because it is used to extract several metals,
including iron, from their oxides: if a metal is less reactive than
carbon, heating its oxide with carbon can be a cheap way of stripping
the oxygen away to leave the metal. (Copper is not actually extracted
this way on an industrial scale — the glowing test-tube is a laboratory
illustration of carbon's position, not a snapshot of a copper works.
Where extraction chemistry goes in detail, Chapter 15 (u2:c15) picks it
up.)

:::did-you-know
Many metals are found in the Earth as metal oxides. Even metals that
occur naturally as other compounds are often converted to oxides first,
before the metal is extracted — the oxide is the standard starting
point for pulling a metal out of its ore.
:::

:::safety
This demonstration needs goggles or a face shield, safety screens, a
well-ventilated room and a bench protected by a large sheet of
hardboard, with everyone at the back of the room. One gram of the
mixture is strongly heated in a metal crown bottle cap; then retire to
the back of the room and wait for the violent reaction. If nothing
happens after a minute or so, turn off the gas, do not touch the
mixture, leave it to cool and dispose of it in water.
:::

:::exam-hint
Displacement answers earn marks in a fixed order: state who is above
whom, apply the rule, name the products, write the equation. For the
carbon reaction, the observation line is worth learning verbatim — the
mixture glows red hot and pink-brown copper is left — because "state
what you would see" questions on this reaction are common and the glow
plus the copper colour are the two observation marks.
:::

:::misconception
"Carbon is a metal because it is in the reactivity series and metals
are the things that react with oxides." Carbon's inclusion is purely
practical: it sits between aluminium and zinc because oxides of metals
below it can be reduced by heating with carbon, which is the basis of
extraction. The series is a ranking of reducing power towards oxygen,
not a club whose membership requires metallic bonding — that is also
why hydrogen, equally a non-metal, gets a slot a few lines further
down.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.16 items. Before moving on, write the two
equations — magnesium with zinc oxide, and carbon with copper(II)
oxide — from memory, and state in each case which substance is
displaced and why. Then predict, without looking anything up, whether
zinc would displace magnesium from magnesium oxide.
:::

sections.title: Oxidation and Reduction
sections.markdown:
Watch the model reaction again, this time through the oxygen:

Mg(s) + CuO(s) → MgO(s) + Cu(s)

A substance has been oxidised if it gains oxygen — the process is
**[[oxidation]]** — and reduced if it loses oxygen, which is
**[[reduction]]**. In this reaction the
magnesium gains oxygen and is oxidised; the copper(II) oxide loses
oxygen and is reduced. Because one substance cannot lose oxygen unless
another simultaneously gains it, the two processes always happen
together, and a reaction in which both are occurring is called a
**[[redox-reaction]]**.

Each reactant also gets an agent's name, and the naming rule is worth
memorising as a pair because it feels backwards at first. The
**[[reducing-agent]]** is the substance that reduces something else: here
the magnesium takes the oxygen away from the copper oxide, reducing it,
so magnesium is the reducing agent. The **[[oxidising-agent]]** is the
substance that oxidises something else: the copper(II) oxide supplies
the oxygen to the magnesium, oxidising it, so copper(II) oxide is the
oxidising agent. Each agent is itself the opposite: an oxidising agent
always gets reduced (it gives away its own oxygen), and a reducing
agent always gets oxidised (it gains the oxygen it removes). The same
assignments follow for the other two competition reactions: in
magnesium with zinc oxide, magnesium is the reducing agent and zinc
oxide the oxidising agent; in carbon with copper(II) oxide, carbon is
the reducing agent and copper(II) oxide the oxidising agent.

Now zoom in to the particles. The magnesium and the copper are metals,
made of atoms; the copper(II) oxide and magnesium oxide are ionic
compounds, made of ions — Cu²⁺ with O²⁻, and Mg²⁺ with O²⁻. Writing the
ions into the equation gives:

Mg(s) + Cu²⁺O²⁻(s) → Mg²⁺O²⁻(s) + Cu(s)

The ion pairs stay paired here because the compounds are solids. Only
when particles are dissolved in solution can their ions move and be
treated separately — in a solid the ions are locked in the lattice.

That solid-lattice lock is exactly why the oxide ion is so revealing.
The oxide ion O²⁻ starts in copper(II) oxide and ends up in magnesium
oxide: it changes partner but is itself completely unchanged. So
oxygen — the thing the first definition is built on — is not actually
the important part of this reaction at all. What really happens is that
magnesium atoms turn into magnesium ions: the atoms lose electrons to
form Mg²⁺, and those electrons transfer to the copper ions. That
prompts a deeper definition of the pair:

- oxidation is loss of electrons
- reduction is gain of electrons

The mnemonic **OILRIG** carries it: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons),
Reduction Is Gain. You now hold two definitions of oxidation and
reduction — one in terms of oxygen, one in terms of electrons — and
both are true.

As a bridge to the next section: when a metal reacts with a solution of
a copper(II) salt, it does not matter which copper(II) salt you chose,
as long as it is soluble — copper(II) chloride or copper(II) nitrate
would react exactly the same way, because the chloride or nitrate ions
would be nothing but spectators: each one a [[spectator-ion]] taking no
part in the reaction. What matters is the copper ion itself.

:::exam-hint
Questions at this level hand you an equation and ask which substance is
oxidised, which is reduced, and which is the agent. Use whichever
definition is simpler for the case in front of you — oxygen movement
for reactions involving oxides, electron movement for ionic equations —
and then apply the agent-reversal rule: the agent is always the
opposite of what it does to the other substance. "The oxidising agent
is reduced" is a complete mark-scheme sentence; learn it.
:::

:::misconception
"The oxidising agent is the substance that gets oxidised." Exactly
backwards. The oxidising agent oxidises *something else* by giving
oxygen to it (or taking electrons from it), so the agent itself is
reduced. Magnesium is oxidised, but copper(II) oxide — the oxidising
agent — is reduced. Candidates who invert this lose the agent mark even
when the oxidation and reduction marks are already banked.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.20 items. Before moving on, take the
reaction Mg(s) + ZnO(s) → MgO(s) + Zn(s) and state, in one sentence
each, which substance is oxidised, which is reduced, which is the
oxidising agent and which is the reducing agent — using the oxygen
definition. Then check the agent-reversal pattern holds.
:::

sections.title: Displacement Reactions Involving Solutions of Salts
sections.markdown:
A **[[salt]]** is a compound such as copper(II) sulfate, silver nitrate
or sodium chloride — the full definition arrives in Chapter 17
(u2:c17), but the family resemblance is enough for now. Salts dissolve
in water to give solutions full of separated ions, and that changes how
displacement works: instead of competing for oxygen inside a solid
oxide, a metal dropped into a salt solution competes for the metal ions
themselves.

Drop zinc into blue copper(II) sulfate solution and the copper is
displaced by the more reactive zinc. The blue colour fades as
colourless zinc sulfate solution forms and pink-brown copper settles
out:

Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)

The zinc and the copper are metals made of atoms; the copper(II)
sulfate and zinc sulfate are ionic. Rewriting the equation with the
ions shown separately makes the ionic story visible:

Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + Cu(s)

Look at the sulfate ions: exactly the same on both sides of the
equation, unchanged by the reaction. They are spectators here — present,
but taking no part. Each one is a **[[spectator-ion]]**: an ion that is
identical on both sides of the equation. Removing them (they do not
belong in the action) leaves:

Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)

This is called an **[[ionic-equation]]**, and it shows only the things
that change. It is also plainly a redox reaction: zinc atoms become
zinc ions, copper ions become copper atoms.

Because everything in solution is already separated, the reaction can
be split into its two halves — the individual oxidation and reduction
processes:

Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻  (oxidation)

Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)  (reduction)

In reality these half-processes cannot occur one without the other: if
something gains electrons, it has to get them from somewhere, so
something else must lose them. The zinc atoms are oxidised to Zn²⁺
because they lose electrons; the Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons and are
reduced to copper atoms.

The agent vocabulary from the oxide reactions translates directly into
electron language. An **oxidising agent** oxidises something else by
taking electrons away from it — oxidising agents accept electrons and
so are reduced themselves. A **reducing agent** reduces something else
by giving electrons to it — reducing agents give away electrons and so
are oxidised themselves. Apply that here: the zinc reduces the Cu²⁺ by
giving electrons to it, so the zinc is the reducing agent — and in the
process it is oxidised, because it gave electrons away. The Cu²⁺
oxidises the zinc by taking electrons away from it, so the Cu²⁺ is the
oxidising agent — and in the process it is reduced, because it took
electrons in.

:::exam-hint
Ionic equations are marked hard on two details: charges must balance as
well as atoms, and state symbols must be there. Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) →
Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) scores because both sides carry charge 2+ and every
species has its state. Writing CuSO₄ instead of Cu²⁺ in the ionic
equation is the classic dropped mark — by the time you have removed the
spectator ions, the sulfate is gone from the answer.
:::

:::misconception
"The sulfate ion reacted, because it changed partner — it ended up
attached to zinc instead of copper." Changing partner is not reacting.
The sulfate ion is identical on both sides of the equation: same
charge, same formula, same state. A [[spectator-ion]] is defined by
taking no part, and the proof is that you can delete every trace of it
from the equation and still have a balanced, truthful statement of the
chemistry.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.16/2.20 items. Before moving on, write the
full equation, the ionic equation and the two half-equations for zinc
reacting with copper(II) sulfate solution, and name the oxidising and
reducing agents in electron terms. That quartet of answers is the
template for every salt-solution question in the topic.
:::

sections.title: The Reaction between Copper and Silver Nitrate Solution
sections.markdown:
Silver sits below copper in the reactivity series, so copper can
displace it — and watching it happen is one of the prettiest
experiments in the course. Stand a coil of copper wire in silver
nitrate solution and metallic silver grows on the wire, as a mixture of
grey "fur" and delicate spiky crystals, while the colourless solution
slowly turns blue. The blue is the tell: copper is dissolving as
copper(II) nitrate as silver leaves the solution.

Cu(s) + 2AgNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2Ag(s)

This time the nitrate ions are the spectators — every one of them a
**[[spectator-ion]]**, identical on both sides — and deleting them from
the equation gives the final version of the
**[[ionic-equation]]**:

Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)

Another redox reaction, of course — every displacement is. The half
story for each element:

Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻  (oxidation)

Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s)  (reduction)

And the agents, in electron terms: the copper is the reducing agent,
because it gives electrons to the Ag⁺ ions to reduce them to silver —
and it is itself oxidised, since it lost those electrons. The Ag⁺ ion
is the oxidising agent, because it takes electrons away from the copper
atoms — and it is itself reduced, since it gained them.

Notice the pattern across the three displacement reactions you have now
met: magnesium with copper(II) oxide, zinc with copper(II) sulfate,
copper with silver nitrate. In each, the more reactive metal starts as
atoms and ends as ions; the less reactive metal starts as ions (or in
an oxide) and ends as atoms. The reactivity series is really a ranking
of how readily a metal surrenders electrons — and every displacement
observation in this chapter is evidence for that ranking.

:::exam-hint
Observation questions love this reaction because it has two changes to
spot, and candidates routinely give only one: the silver deposit on the
wire (grey fur or crystals) AND the solution turning blue. Both carry
marks. If you also call the deposit "silver mirrors", fine — but the
safe description is grey coating/spiky crystals of silver metal on the
copper.
:::

:::misconception
"The solution turns blue because the silver is dissolving into it." The
silver does the opposite of dissolving — it leaves the solution as
metal. The blue colour belongs to the copper(II) ions forming as copper
atoms become Cu²⁺. Colour evidence has an owner: blue solutions here
mean Cu²⁺(aq), and attributing the colour to the wrong metal costs the
observation mark even when the equation is perfect.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.16/2.20 items. Before moving on, write the
ionic equation for copper reacting with silver nitrate solution,
identify the spectator ion, and state which metal is the reducing
agent. Then predict: would silver displace copper from copper(II)
sulfate solution?
:::

sections.title: Metals Above Hydrogen in the Reacti Metals Above Hydrogen in the Reactivity Series
sections.markdown:
The second half of the chapter ranks metals a different way: by how
they treat water and dilute acids. Hydrogen is the dividing line, and
this section takes everything above it.

Metals above hydrogen in the **[[reactivity-series]]** react with water
(or steam) and produce hydrogen gas. The product depends on which form
of water you use:

metal + cold water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen

metal + steam → metal oxide + hydrogen

Cold water leaves the metal as its hydroxide; steam — water too hot to
survive as a hydroxide-forming environment — leaves the oxide. The
hydrogen product is the same in both cases, which is what makes these
reactions such clean tests: collect the gas, apply a lighted splint,
hear the squeaky pop.

One more pattern rides along: as you move down the reactivity series,
the reactions become less and less vigorous. Potassium dices with cold
water at the top of the ladder; magnesium barely argues with it;
somewhere below hydrogen the argument stops altogether. That vigour
gradient is not decoration — it is the evidence an examiner asks you to
rank metals with, and the next several sections walk down it metal by
metal.

:::exam-hint
The hydroxide-versus-oxide product split is a marking point in its own
right. Cold water questions want "metal hydroxide + hydrogen"; steam
questions want "metal oxide + hydrogen". Answering a steam equation
with a hydroxide is one of the most common product errors in this
topic — the water's state symbol (g) in steam equations is the visual
cue that the oxide rule applies.
:::

:::misconception
"If a metal does not react visibly with cold water, it must be below
hydrogen." Not so. Magnesium is well above hydrogen yet barely reacts
with cold water, because it coats itself in insoluble magnesium
hydroxide that shuts the reaction down (and aluminium's oxide layer
does the same job). Cold-water silence is not a verdict — it is one
data point that later sections teach you to test with steam and then
with acids before any ranking is assigned.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15 items. Before moving on, write the two
general word equations — metal with cold water, metal with steam — and
state the gas both produce and the test for it. Those two lines are the
skeleton of every water-reaction answer in this chapter.
:::

sections.title: Metals Below Hydrogen in the Reactivity Series
sections.markdown:
Metals below hydrogen do not react with water or steam — no hydroxide,
no oxide, no hydrogen, however long you wait. This is why copper can be
used for both hot and cold water pipes: water flowing through copper
all day, every day, at every temperature a household can produce,
never reacts with it. The pipes last decades because the chemistry
simply refuses to start.

The same below-hydrogen rule explains the precious metals. Gold stays
untarnished in air and water indefinitely; silver keeps its shine far
better than base metals; platinum survives everything a laboratory can
throw at it. Where a metal sits relative to hydrogen decides whether
water is a threat to it or just a spectator.

The top of the series, by contrast, is a place where water reactions
are violent. The reactions of potassium, sodium and lithium with cold
water are described in full in Chapter 11 (u2:c11) — very vigorous,
though becoming less violent in the order potassium > sodium > lithium.
Here in Chapter 14, those reactions return as ranking evidence: the
fact that potassium, sodium and lithium all react briskly with cold
water while magnesium waits for steam is itself an ordering statement,
and the general equation for their cold-water reactions opens the next
section.

:::exam-hint
Application questions pair below-hydrogen chemistry with a use:
"copper is used for water pipes — explain why". The mark scheme wants
two steps: copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it
does not react with water (or steam); therefore the pipes do not
corrode away/react away. Naming the position AND the consequence earns
both marks; naming only "unreactive" is treated as incomplete.
:::

:::misconception
"Copper is completely inert — nothing can react with it." Below
hydrogen means no reaction with water or steam; it does not mean no
reactions at all. Copper yields to the displacement reactions earlier
in this chapter — silver nitrate takes electrons from copper atoms —
and it combines with oxygen on heating. The series is a ranking of
specific reactivities, not a certificate of general inertness.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15 items. Before moving on, name two metals
that do not react with water or steam, state where they sit in the
reactivity series relative to hydrogen, and give one everyday use that
follows from that position.
:::

sections.title: Reaction of Calcium with Cold Water
sections.markdown:
Potassium, sodium and lithium react with cold water to give the metal
hydroxide and hydrogen, and their equations all share one shape:

2M(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2MOH(aq) + H₂(g)

Replace M by K, Na or Li, depending on which metal you want. Calcium is
the next rung down, and it behaves like a gentler member of the same
family. Calcium reacts with cold water steadily rather than violently:
the grey granules sink, but bubbles of hydrogen form around them and
carry them back to the surface, and the mixture becomes warm as heat is
produced. The product is calcium hydroxide, which is only slightly
soluble — some dissolves to give a colourless solution, but most of it
is left behind as a white, insoluble solid:

Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq or s) + H₂(g)

Magnesium, one rung below calcium, shows how quickly the vigour fades.
In cold water there is almost no reaction: if the magnesium is very
clean, a few bubbles of hydrogen form on it, but the reaction soon
stops, because the magnesium becomes coated with insoluble magnesium
hydroxide that blocks any more water from reaching the metal surface.

Steam changes the picture. Magnesium ribbon heated in steam — the wet
mineral wool at the bottom of the tube supplies water, and the heat
applied to the middle of the tube turns that water to steam which
passes over the hot metal — burns with a bright white flame, and the
hydrogen produced can be ignited at the end of the delivery tube. White
magnesium oxide is formed:

Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g)

Two details from this apparatus are worth carrying forward. The mineral
wool is not heated directly: enough heat conducts back along the
test-tube to turn the water to steam. And water in these equations
carries the state symbol (g), because you are dealing with it as steam.

One metal seems missing from the story. Aluminium's reactivity should
place it between magnesium and zinc, yet it has only a very slow
reaction with steam. The reason is a very thin but very strong layer of
aluminium oxide on the metal's surface: aluminium only shows its true
reactivity if that layer is penetrated, and water and steam are poor at
penetrating it. Hold that thought — the acid reactions later in the
chapter tell the same story.

:::safety
Care must be taken during the steam experiment to avoid "suck-back":
stop heating only once the delivery tube is out of the water, because
water can be sucked back into the hot tube while it cools — and a
sudden dose of cold water often cracks the glass.
:::

:::exam-hint
Calcium-plus-cold-water observation questions have four standard marks:
bubbles of hydrogen (effervescence), the metal rises/floats on its own
bubbles, the mixture gets warm, and a white insoluble solid (or slightly
cloudy mixture) of calcium hydroxide forms. Learn them as a set — the
question usually allows three, and knowing four protects you when one
phrasing escapes you under pressure.
:::

:::misconception
"Calcium must be less reactive than sodium because its reaction with
water is so much calmer." It is less reactive — but the observation is
misleading on its own, because both metals react the same way in
principle and vigour is the only visible difference. The comparison
only becomes a ranking statement when the reactions are run side by
side under the same conditions; on its own, "gentle fizzing" tells you
calcium is lower than sodium but not where it stands against, say,
magnesium. Rankings come from comparisons, not from single
observations.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15 items. Before moving on, write the
balanced equation for calcium with cold water, name the product and
state its solubility behaviour, then explain in one sentence why
magnesium shows almost no reaction with cold water but burns brightly
in steam.
:::

sections.title: With Zinc
sections.markdown:
Zinc and iron also react with steam — slowly enough that the hydrogen
comes off and can be collected, and neither metal burns. With zinc, the
oxide forms; zinc oxide is yellow when hot but white on cooling:

Zn(s) + H₂O(g) → ZnO(s) + H₂(g)

With iron, the metal darkens slightly and a complicated oxide called
**[[tri-iron-tetroxide]]**, Fe₃O₄, is produced:

3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)

Metals below hydrogen — copper among them — react with neither water
nor steam, so the water ladder ends here. But water is only half of the
ranking toolkit. The other half is dilute acids, and this is where the
chapter's listed practical lives.

**The practical: metals with dilute acids.** Set up four test-tubes
with about 2 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid in each, and drop a small
piece of magnesium, zinc, iron or copper into each. Watch for a
reaction; where there is fizzing, collect or trap the gas and apply a
lighted splint — a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen. Then repeat the whole
set with dilute sulfuric acid. With hydrochloric acid the results come
out like this:

| Metal | Reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid |
|---|---|
| Magnesium | Reacts vigorously with lots of fizzing. The gas gave a squeaky pop with a lighted splint. A colourless solution forms. The test-tube gets hot. |
| Zinc | Steady reaction with fizzing. Enough gas eventually collects to give a squeaky pop. A colourless solution forms. The test-tube gets warmer. |
| Iron | Slow fizzing. Very little gas collects in the time available. A very pale green solution forms. The test-tube gets slightly warmer. |
| Copper | No change. |

All of these reactions are exothermic — they give out heat (Chapter 19,
u3:c19, develops exothermic reactions properly). That temperature rise
is not just a detail: it is a measuring opportunity. If magnesium warms
the tube most and copper not at all, the temperature change could rank
the metals quantitatively. To compare metals this way, though, the test
has to be a **[[valid-test]]** — every variable except the metal held
constant — and the obvious control exposes a subtlety.

Equal masses are not equal amounts. 0.24 g of magnesium is
0.24/24 = 0.010 mol, but 0.24 g of iron is 0.24/56 = 0.0040 mol.
Chemical reactions depend on how many particles are present, so the
same mass gives the magnesium experiment more moles — and more
particles — and therefore more heat given out, for reasons that have
nothing to do with reactivity. The comparison must use the same number
of **moles** in each experiment, not the same number of grams.

One more variable: surface area. It does not change the total heat
given out, but it changes how fast the heat is released — and a slow
reaction spreads its heat over a long time, losing more of it to the
surroundings, which drags the measured temperature change down. Metal
powders, with their large surface area, keep the reaction quick and the
heat loss small (rate of reaction is Chapters 19 and 20's territory,
u3:c19 and u3:c20).

The full quantitative procedure: measure out 50 cm³ of 1 mol/dm³
hydrochloric acid with a measuring cylinder — chosen so the acid is in
excess, more than enough to react with all of the metal in every case.
Measure the initial temperature of the acid. Weigh out 0.010 mol of
magnesium powder (0.010 × 24 = 0.24 g). Add the powder to the acid, fit
the lid, stir, and record the maximum temperature reached. Repeat with
the other metals, 0.010 mol each time. Typical data:

| Metal | Mass/g | Initial temperature/°C | Maximum temperature/°C |
|---|---|---|---|
| magnesium | 0.24 | 18 | 40 |
| zinc | 0.65 | 19 | 26 |
| iron | 0.56 | 18 | 22 |
| copper | 0.64 | 18 | 18 |

The temperature rise for each experiment is maximum minus initial, and
the four rises are best displayed as a bar chart — the type of metal is
not continuous data (a metal is magnesium or zinc, never something in
between), so a line graph would claim a continuity the chemistry does
not have. (For completeness: the molar enthalpy change of each reaction
could also be calculated — Chapter 19, u3:c19, shows how.)

One boundary on all of this: the trends here apply to simple acids such
as dilute sulfuric or dilute hydrochloric acid. Nitric acid and
concentrated sulfuric acid behave completely differently with most
metals — those reactions are problems beyond International GCSE.

:::safety
Wear eye protection. Keep hands and face away from the mouths of the
tubes: some acid aerosol — tiny droplets of acid — can be carried out
of the tube by the escaping gas.
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection and avoid splashing the acid when stirring — the
stirring step that follows the powder addition is the moment most
likely to throw droplets.
:::

:::maths-skills
The fair-comparison arithmetic is the examinable quantitative core.
Convert mass to moles with moles = mass/Mᵣ: 0.24/24 = 0.010 mol of
magnesium (Mᵣ = 24), 0.24/56 = 0.0040 mol of iron (Mᵣ = 56) — equal
masses, unequal moles. Then compute each temperature rise by
subtraction: magnesium 40 − 18 = 22 °C, zinc 26 − 19 = 7 °C, iron
22 − 18 = 4 °C, copper 18 − 18 = 0 °C. Choosing 0.010 mol for every
metal makes the only difference between the experiments the metal
itself — which is what "valid test" means, arithmetically.
:::

:::exam-hint
The listed practical is examined twice over: a describe-the-method
question (volume and concentration of acid, initial temperature, mass
or moles of metal, maximum temperature, control variables) and a
why-same-moles question (same mass gives different moles; reactions
depend on number of particles). The in-excess point is a regular
follow-up: the acid is in excess so that all the metal reacts in every
experiment — otherwise the metal, not its reactivity, would limit the
heat given out.
:::

:::misconception
"Using the same mass of each metal makes the comparison fair, because
fairness means keeping everything equal." Equality of the wrong
quantity is inequality in disguise. Equal masses contain different
numbers of moles — 0.010 mol of magnesium against 0.0040 mol of iron —
so the heat given out differs because of amount, not reactivity. A
[[valid-test]] controls the variable that matters chemically (moles of
metal, acid volume and concentration, surface area), not the one that
merely looks equal on the balance.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.21/2.15 items. Before moving on, write the
equations for zinc with steam and iron with steam (including the state
symbol for water), then set out the four control variables for the
temperature-change practical and the reason each is held constant.
:::

sections.title: Metals Above Hydrogen in the Reactivity Series
sections.markdown:
The acids half of the ranking story reuses the water half's dividing
line exactly. Metals above hydrogen in the **reactivity series** react
with dilute acids and produce hydrogen; the product that joins the
hydrogen is a salt, which makes the whole pattern one line long. There
is a mnemonic for it, and it is worth adopting permanently:

**MASH** — Metal + Acid → Salt + Hydrogen.

Say the pattern rather than memorising dozens of individual reactions:
every metal-acid equation you will write in this course is MASH with
the names filled in, and the salt's name comes automatically from the
acid (sulfuric acid gives sulfates, hydrochloric acid gives chlorides —
the next sections fill the table in). The hydrogen, meanwhile, is the
same squeaky-pop gas the water reactions produced, so the test carries
over unchanged.

As with water, being above hydrogen is the ticket: the higher the
metal, the more violent the reaction, and the metals below hydrogen sit
the acid reactions out entirely. The next sections walk the series
through that story — first the metals too reactive to try, then the
middle order where the teaching examples live, then the general summary
that turns the pattern into equations.

:::exam-hint
MASH earns its keep under exam pressure: write it down first, then
substitute the metal and the acid, and the salt name suggests itself
from the acid's family. Examiners accept the mnemonic as working
provided the final equation is complete with state symbols — the
mnemonic is scaffolding, not the answer.
:::

:::misconception
"Acid strength and metal position are two independent factors you must
weigh up." For the dilute acids of this course, the metal's position
decides everything: above hydrogen reacts, below hydrogen does not, and
vigour climbs with position. The acid's identity only chooses the salt
half of the product. Treating the acid as a variable to negotiate with
produces hedged answers ("might react, depending on the acid") where
the mark scheme wants a decision.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15 items. Before moving on, unpack MASH in
full — what each letter stands for, which side of the hydrogen line a
metal must sit on, and how the salt's name is obtained from the acid's
name.
:::

sections.title: Metals Below Hydrogen in the Reactivity Series
sections.markdown:
The acids narrative splits the above-hydrogen metals into three
neighbourhoods, and knowing the boundaries is as useful as knowing any
individual metal. Below hydrogen: copper, silver and gold do not react
with simple dilute acids such as sulfuric or hydrochloric acid at all —
the MASH pattern never starts. At the very top: potassium, sodium,
lithium and calcium. These are too reactive to add safely to acids —
the reaction is far too violent — which is why no school laboratory
drops potassium into dilute hydrochloric acid. Calcium bends the rule
only slightly: it can be used if the acid is very dilute. In the
middle, from magnesium down to iron: the orderly gradient where the
teaching examples live, vigorous for magnesium and settling to a slow
fizz for iron.

So the acid-based ranking of a familiar set of metals reads: the
top four are ruled by safety rather than by observation; magnesium,
aluminium, zinc and iron can be compared directly by vigour; copper,
silver and gold cannot enter the comparison at all. Keep those three
neighbourhoods in mind and every "which metal reacts faster" question
becomes a placement exercise.

The stirring steps in these experiments carry the usual acid-splash
discipline — droplets of acid travel further than students expect.

:::safety
Wear eye protection and avoid splashing the acid when stirring. The
metals above calcium are never added to acids in a school laboratory:
with potassium, sodium or lithium the reaction is dangerously violent.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain why potassium is never added to dilute acid in a school
laboratory" is a one-mark gift if you know the neighbourhood map: the
answer is the violence of the reaction at the top of the series, not
the acid's danger. Candidates who answer "because the acid is too
concentrated" have the chemistry upside down — the acid is ordinary;
the metal is extreme.
:::

:::misconception
"Copper does not react with dilute acids because the acid is too weak
to attack it." The acid's strength is not the deciding variable —
dilute acid happily attacks magnesium and zinc. Copper sits below
hydrogen in the reactivity series, and that position, not any property
of the acid, closes the reaction down. Swap the acid for a stronger
one of the same simple type and copper still declines; swap copper for
magnesium and even a weak start fizzes.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15 items. Before moving on, name one metal
from each of the three neighbourhoods — too violent with acids, orderly
middle, no reaction — and state the neighbourhood rule each one
illustrates.
:::

sections.title: Temperature Changes When Metals React with Hydrochloric Acid
sections.markdown:
The temperature-change data from the practical converts directly into a
ranking. Magnesium caused the greatest temperature change, so it is the
most reactive metal of the four tested; copper caused no change at all,
so it is the least reactive. In between, zinc's 7 °C rise beats iron's
4 °C, and the practical's four metals drop into an order — magnesium,
zinc, iron, copper — without anyone having to observe a single fizz.

That is the quiet power of the quantitative method: the temperature
change acts as a reactivity meter. A bigger rise under controlled
conditions means a more vigorous reaction means a more reactive metal,
and the graph summarises in one picture what a table of observations
can only suggest. The bar chart also makes the copper result vivid —
zero rise, no bar — which is exactly what "below hydrogen, no reaction"
looks like when it is plotted.

The ranking earned here is approximate, and that word matters. Vigour
depends on the metal's position, but also on its surface area and
whether its surface is clean — the next sections put error bars around
the whole method.

:::exam-hint
Data-interpretation questions on this experiment ask for the conclusion
AND the reasoning in one chain: "magnesium caused the greatest
temperature change, so it is the most reactive of the four." Answers
that state the ranking without citing the temperature-change evidence
leave the reasoning mark behind — the measurement is the argument.
:::

:::misconception
"Copper's flat bar means the experiment failed for copper — a fair test
should show something." A zero is a result. Copper is below hydrogen,
so no reaction occurs, no heat is released, and the temperature stays
exactly where it started. Reading a null result as equipment error —
rather than as evidence for the metal's position — inverts the most
useful lesson of the quantitative method.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15/2.21 items. Before moving on, state the
ranking of the four practical metals from the temperature data and
identify which result is a null measurement — and what that null
tells you about the metal's position in the series.
:::

sections.title: A General Summary
sections.markdown:
The acid reactions follow the same pattern as the water reactions, but
each one is much more vigorous. Metals above hydrogen react with acids
to form a **[[salt]]** and hydrogen, and the higher the metal, the more
violent the reaction:

metal + dilute sulfuric acid → metal sulfate + hydrogen

metal + dilute hydrochloric acid → metal chloride + hydrogen

The top and bottom of the series behave as the last two sections
established: metals such as copper, silver and gold do not react with
simple dilute acids, while potassium, sodium and lithium are too
reactive to add safely — calcium only joins in if the acid is very
dilute.

Magnesium reacts vigorously with cold dilute acids and the mixture
becomes hot, leaving a colourless solution of magnesium sulfate or
magnesium chloride. With dilute sulfuric acid:

Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)

Aluminium is the spoiler in the middle of the series. Its reactivity
should place it above zinc, yet in the cold it barely reacts with
dilute acids — the same thin, strong oxide layer that muted its
reaction with steam stands in the way. The acid removes that layer, and
once it is gone the aluminium shows its true reactivity. With dilute
hydrochloric acid:

2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g)

Zinc and iron react slowly in the cold but more rapidly on heating,
with vigour less than aluminium's. Zinc forms zinc sulfate or zinc
chloride and hydrogen; iron forms iron(II) sulfate or iron(II)
chloride — the iron(II) family, carrying Fe²⁺ ions, not the iron(III)
family. For example:

Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) → FeCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)

Two cautions keep this summary honest. First, the placement this method
gives is approximate: how vigorously a metal reacts with a dilute acid
depends on its position in the series, but also on its surface area and
on whether the surface is free from dirt or an oxide coating. A dirty
or oxide-armoured metal underperforms its true position. Second, the
method needs the ion charges before any products can be named and
formulated — you need to know the charge on the ion to deduce the
formulae of the compounds, and if the charge-deduction routine is
rusty, Chapter 7 (u1:c07) is the place to sharpen it.

:::key-point
There are two ranges of iron salts — one containing Fe²⁺ ions and one
containing Fe³⁺ ions. These acid reactions produce iron(II) salts,
containing Fe²⁺. Writing FeCl₃ or Fe₂(SO₄)₃ as the product of iron with
a dilute acid names the wrong family.
:::

:::exam-hint
The aluminium narrative is a favourite examination story because it
tests two ideas at once: the oxide layer that hides aluminium's true
reactivity (why the cold reaction is so slow) and the acid's job of
stripping that layer (why the reaction then accelerates). Equations for
aluminium need the extra balancing care — 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂ —
because the +3 ion drags the ratios up. Balance atoms first, then
check the hydrogens last.
:::

:::misconception
"Iron with dilute sulfuric acid makes iron(III) sulfate, because iron
rusts to iron(III)." Rusting and acid reaction are different processes
with different products: the acid reaction produces iron(II) salts
(Fe²⁺) — a pale green solution with dilute sulfuric acid is iron(II)
sulfate forming. The iron(III) family belongs to other chemistry.
Reaching for the more familiar iron(III) name is the single most common
product error in this section.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15/2.21 items. Before moving on, write
balanced equations with state symbols for magnesium with dilute
sulfuric acid, aluminium with dilute hydrochloric acid and iron with
dilute hydrochloric acid — naming each salt correctly — and explain in
one sentence why aluminium underperforms in the cold.
:::

sections.title: Finding the Approximate Position of a Metal in the Reactivity Series Using Water and Dilute Acids
sections.markdown:
Everything the chapter has built — the water reactions, the acid
reactions, the vigour gradient — compresses into a four-step decision
procedure that places an unknown metal approximately in the
**reactivity series** using nothing but water and dilute acid:

1. Add a very small piece of the metal to some cold water. Any rapid
   reaction places the metal above magnesium in the series.
2. If there is no reaction, add a small amount of the metal to some
   dilute hydrochloric acid (or dilute sulfuric acid), cold.
3. If there is still no reaction in the cold acid, warm it carefully.
   A reaction at this stage places the metal somewhere between
   magnesium and hydrogen.
4. If even the warmed acid does nothing, the metal is probably below
   hydrogen.

The procedure is a bisection: water cuts the series at magnesium,
cold acid cuts it again, warm acid sweeps out the sluggish middle, and
silence everywhere leaves only the below-hydrogen neighbourhood. It
gives a bracket, not a coordinate — "between magnesium and hydrogen" or
"above magnesium" — but a bracket is usually all a prediction needs,
and the safety ordering is built into the sequence: water before acid,
cold before warm, tiny pieces throughout.

:::exam-hint
Describe-the-method questions on this procedure are marked on ORDER.
Water before acid and cold before warm are not stylistic preferences —
they are the safety logic and the discrimination logic of the test at
once. An answer that starts with warmed concentrated acid has invented
a hazard and lost the sequence marks; the procedure only needs the two
reagents named in the chapter and a stepwise "if no reaction, then…"
chain.
:::

:::misconception
"A metal that fizzes in cold dilute acid must be above magnesium,
because fizzing means very reactive." Fizzing in acid only proves the
metal is above hydrogen — magnesium is the reference point the cold
water test uses, not the acid test. Zinc fizzes steadily in dilute acid
and sits below magnesium; iron fizzes slowly and sits lower still. The
two tests work together: water brackets the top of the series, acid
sorts everything between magnesium and hydrogen.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15 items. Before moving on, recite the
four-step procedure from memory and state the bracket conclusion at
each step. Then apply it: an unknown metal shows no reaction with cold
water, no reaction with cold dilute hydrochloric acid, but fizzes when
the acid is warmed — where does it sit?
:::

sections.title: Making Predictions Using the Reactivity Series
sections.markdown:
A ranking you cannot use to predict is just trivia. The payoff of
knowing the order of reactivity — potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium,
magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold — is
that unfamiliar metals become solvable on sight: fix their position,
apply the displacement rule, name the products, write the equation.
The chapter's worked example shows the machinery on a metal most
students have never seen in a bottle.

:::worked-example
Manganese (Mn) lies between aluminium and zinc in the reactivity
series, and forms a 2+ ion. Solutions of manganese(II) salts are very
pale pink, almost colourless.

**(a)** Use the reactivity series to predict whether manganese will
react with copper(II) sulfate solution. If it will react, describe what
you would see, name the products and write an equation for the
reaction.

**(b)** Explain why you would expect manganese to react with steam.
Name the products of the reaction and write the equation.

The method, before the answers: place manganese on the ladder (between
aluminium and zinc puts it above zinc, iron, hydrogen and copper);
apply the displacement rule twice (above copper means it takes copper's
place in a salt solution; above hydrogen means it reacts with steam);
deduce the products from position and ion charge (a 2+ ion means
manganese(II) compounds, so the sulfate product is MnSO₄ and the steam
product is MnO). The next two sections deliver the full answers — part
(a) as a displacement observation, part (b) as a steam-reaction
equation.
:::

The same predictive logic powers one of the most famous reactions in
everyday chemistry: rusting. Before the chapter closes on it, two
precisions. First, a naming discipline: many metals corrode, but only
the corrosion of iron is called rusting — zinc, copper and aluminium
corrode, but they do not rust. Second, the chemistry underneath: forming
rust from iron is a surprisingly complicated process. The iron loses
electrons to form iron(II) ions, Fe²⁺, which are then oxidised by the
air to iron(III) ions, Fe³⁺; reactions involving water then produce the
actual rust. Rusting is redox from the first atom lost — which is why
it belongs to this chapter, and why the ways of stopping it are ways of
blocking electron and oxygen chemistry, not just weatherproofing.

:::key-point
Rust formation is a chain, not a single step: Fe → Fe²⁺ (iron loses
electrons) → Fe³⁺ (air oxidises it further) → hydrated iron(III) oxide
with water's help. Both oxygen and water are needed, and both terms of
that requirement are examinable.
:::

:::exam-hint
Prediction questions are marked on the chain: position → decision →
observation → products → equation. Practise saying the position out
loud first ("manganese is above copper because it lies between
aluminium and zinc, and copper is below iron") — the position sentence
is a marking point in its own right, and it forces the decision to be
right by construction.
:::

:::misconception
"You cannot predict anything about a metal you have never met —
predictions need experiments on the actual metal." That is backwards:
experiments on the actual metal are what the prediction spares you. Two
facts of position (between aluminium and zinc; forms 2+ ions) are
enough to decide both of the manganese questions before any glassware
is touched. The series is an interpolation device — its whole economic
value is converting a few careful measurements into thousands of
confident predictions.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.17/2.18 items. Before moving on, restate the
manganese setup in your own words and predict, before reading the next
section, what you would observe when manganese meets copper(II) sulfate
solution — deposit, colour change, products. Check yourself against the
worked answer that follows.
:::

sections.title: Preventing Rusting by Using Barriers
sections.markdown:
Rusting needs two reactants — oxygen and water — and the most obvious
way to stop it is to keep one or both of them away from the iron. That
is the whole logic of the **[[barrier-method]]** family: put a
water-and-air-proof layer between the iron and the world.

Painting is the everyday answer, and oil or grease works for moving
parts where paint would flake; covering with plastic suits everything
from garden furniture to dishwasher racks. A slightly less obvious
member of the family is coating the iron with a metal *below* iron in
the reactivity series — coating steel with tin for food cans is the
standard example. The tin is unreactive enough to act as the barrier
itself.

Barrier methods are usually cheap, which is why they dominate wherever
the coating is likely to stay intact. Their weakness is built in: once
the coating is broken, the iron underneath is exposed to oxygen and
water and rusting starts — and rust spreads under the coating, so even
areas away from the scratch end up under attack. A barrier is only as
good as its continuity, which is why the two methods in the next
sections — galvanising and sacrificial protection — exist: they keep
protecting the iron even when things get scratched.

:::exam-hint
"Give two ways of preventing rusting" is a recall gift, but the
follow-up "explain how each works" separates the grades: every barrier
answer must name what is being kept away — oxygen and water. Paint
prevents rusting *because* it excludes air and moisture, not because
paint has magic anti-rust properties. Tin-plating answers must also
flag that tin is BELOW iron in the series — that position is why tin
plating is a barrier method only, a distinction the next sections
exploit.
:::

:::misconception
"Any metal coating protects iron from rusting." The metal's position in
the reactivity series decides what kind of protection you get. Tin,
below iron, protects only while it is unbroken — once scratched, the
iron rusts away under the hole. Zinc, above iron, protects even when
scratched, because the zinc corrodes in iron's place. Same idea, same
can-shaped result, opposite failure modes — and examiners set the tin
versus zinc comparison precisely to test whether you know which is
which.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.19 items. Before moving on, name three
barrier methods and state the two substances each one keeps away from
the iron. Then predict what happens to a scratched tin can compared
with a scratched galvanised sheet — the next sections supply the
mechanism.
:::

sections.title: A the Reaction between Manganese and Copper(ii) Sulfate Solution
sections.markdown:
**Part (a), answered.** Manganese is above copper in the reactivity
series — it lies between aluminium and zinc, and copper is below iron —
so it will react, displacing copper from the copper(II) sulfate
solution. This is a [[displacement-reaction]], and every observation in
it follows from who is gaining and who is losing:

- a pink-brown deposit of copper forms on the manganese;
- the blue colour of the copper(II) sulfate solution fades, ending as a
  very pale pink — virtually colourless — solution of manganese(II)
  sulfate;
- the equation, built from Mn²⁺ and the sulfate ion:

Mn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → MnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)

Notice how the setup facts did all the work. "Between aluminium and
zinc" placed manganese above copper; "forms a 2+ ion" named the
products (manganese(II) sulfate, MnSO₄); "very pale pink, almost
colourless" gave the final solution colour. Nothing was measured — the
prediction was executed from position alone, exactly as the reactivity
series intends.

:::exam-hint
Full-mark answers to part (a) carry four marking points: the decision
(will react, because manganese is above copper), the observation pair
(pink-brown deposit AND fading blue solution), the product names
(copper + manganese(II) sulfate) and the balanced equation. The
observation pair is the most commonly dropped — candidates who write
"it reacts" without saying what appears have banked the decision and
abandoned the description marks.
:::

:::misconception
"The product is manganese(III) sulfate or manganese(IV) sulfate —
transition metals have lots of charges, so any of them could be right."
The setup specified manganese forms a 2+ ion, which fixes the formula
as MnSO₄ and the name as manganese(II) sulfate — one manganese ion
balancing one 2− sulfate ion. Reading the given ion charge before
naming products is the difference between a prediction and a guess;
for unfamiliar metals, the charge is always supplied for exactly this
reason.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.16/2.17 items. Before moving on, write the
part (a) answer from memory — decision, both observations, both product
names, equation — and check each marking point against the section.
:::

sections.title: B the Reaction between Manganese and Steam
sections.markdown:
**Part (b), answered.** Manganese sits above hydrogen in the reactivity
series, and metals above hydrogen react with steam to give hydrogen and
the metal oxide — so manganese is expected to react. The products are
hydrogen and the metal oxide, which for a 2+ ion is manganese(II)
oxide:

Mn(s) + H₂O(g) → MnO(s) + H₂(g)

One sentence in the model answer deserves as much attention as the
chemistry: you could not predict the colour of the manganese(II) oxide,
and the question does not ask you to do this. Position predicts reaction
behaviour — that a reaction happens and what the products are. It does
not hand you every physical property of the products, and inventing a
colour for an oxide you have never seen is not prediction; it is
fabrication with confidence. A prediction answer that stops exactly
where its evidence stops is a complete answer.

:::exam-hint
The steam products rule does the work here: metal + steam → metal oxide
+ hydrogen, with the oxidation number supplied by the setup (2+ ion →
MnO). The discipline to copy is the stopping rule: answer what was
asked. If a question wants products and an equation, properties not
requested — colour, density, smell — add nothing and risk everything.
:::

:::misconception
"Metals above hydrogen make hydroxides with steam, just like they do
with cold water." Cold water gives the hydroxide; steam gives the
oxide — the state of the water decides the product family. Writing
Mn(OH)₂ plus hydrogen for a steam reaction mixes the two product rules
and loses the product mark even though the decision to react was
correct. Watch the state symbol on the water: (g) means steam rules.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.15 items. Before moving on, write the part
(b) answer — the reason manganese reacts with steam, both product
names, and the balanced equation with state symbols — and note the one
property the model answer refuses to predict.
:::

sections.title: Rusting of Iron
sections.markdown:
Iron rusts in the presence of oxygen and water — both, together, or not
at all. Rusting affects iron and its most common alloy, mild steel,
and the product is hydrated iron(III) oxide, whose formula is written
Fe₂O₃·xH₂O with x a variable number of waters of crystallisation.
**Rusting** is a redox process: the iron is oxidised, exactly
as the electron story of the worked example predicted — Fe to Fe²⁺ to
Fe³⁺, with water's reactions producing the actual solid. Salt speeds
**[[rusting]]** up, which is why vehicles near salty roads and boats in
seawater corrode with such enthusiasm.

**Barriers** — the first line of defence — were the last section's
subject: paint, oil or grease, plastic, or a coating of a metal below
iron such as tin. They work by exclusion and fail by scratching.

**Galvanising** is the upgrade. **Galvanised iron** — iron coated with a
layer of zinc, a process called **[[galvanising]]** — behaves like an
ordinary barrier to air and water while the zinc layer is unscratched.
The remarkable part is
what happens when the coating IS scratched: the iron still does not
rust. Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series, so it reacts with
oxygen and water more readily than the iron does — the zinc corrodes
instead of the iron, even where the exposed patch is far from the
remaining zinc. The extension view shows the mechanism: the zinc loses
electrons (is oxidised) to form zinc ions, Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻, and
those electrons flow into the iron. Any iron atom that has lost
electrons to form an ion immediately regains them — and if the iron
cannot form ions, it cannot rust. In galvanised steel, the zinc's
electrons prevent the ionisation of the iron; magnesium worked into the
protection corrodes in preference to the iron for the same reason.

**Sacrificial protection** generalises that trick. Zinc, magnesium or
aluminium blocks are attached to the metal hulls or keels of ships to
prevent the iron or steel from rusting. For it to work, the block must
be a metal more reactive than iron: the more reactive metal reacts (is
oxidised) more readily in the presence of oxygen and water, and its
corrosion prevents the iron from rusting. The blocks are called
**sacrificial anodes** — the technique is **[[sacrificial-protection]]**
— and they have to be
replaced occasionally, once all the more reactive metal has been
oxidised. This is the protection of choice on large structures —
pipelines, piers, ship hulls — where a barrier coating would be
impossible to keep continuous. Galvanising itself is best understood as
a combination: a barrier method while intact, sacrificial protection
wherever it is scratched.

The exam-facing summary of the whole defence: keep oxygen and water
away (barriers); or coat with a more reactive metal that corrodes
first (galvanising, sacrificial anodes). Choose by circumstance —
barriers where the coating stays whole and cheap matters; sacrificial
metal where scratching is guaranteed and the structure is too large to
paint perfectly.

:::cross-curricular
This chapter's chemistry runs heavy industry. The rail-welding reaction
that opened it — aluminium taking oxygen from iron(III) oxide — is
thermite welding, done trackside with no furnace. Tin-plated steel
cans keep food safe by barrier chemistry alone. Ship hulls carry
sacrificial anodes that marine engineers size and replace on a
schedule, converting a reactivity ranking into a maintenance budget;
and the discipline of protecting iron structures predates the electron
explanation by a century — the chemistry of Chapter 9 (u1:c09) explains
what centuries of shipwrights already knew worked.
:::

:::exam-hint
Prevention questions are comparison questions in disguise. The safe
template: name the method, state what it keeps away or what it supplies
(oxygen and water for barriers; electrons via a more reactive metal for
galvanising/sacrificial), and match the method to the scenario (barrier
for cans and railings; galvanising for outdoor steel that gets
scratched; sacrificial anodes for ships and pipelines). "Explain why
galvanised iron does not rust even when scratched" wants the electron
sentence: zinc is more reactive, corrodes preferentially, and the
electrons it releases prevent the iron from forming ions.
:::

:::misconception
"A galvanised coating is just a fancy paint — once it is scratched, the
iron underneath rusts like any other scratched barrier." That is true
of tin and false of zinc, and the difference is the entire point:
galvanising's zinc is above iron, so a scratch hands the corrosion job
to the coating rather than to the iron. The protection does not switch
off when the coating is breached — it relocates. Candidates who
classify galvanising as barrier-only lose the explanation mark on
every scratched-coating follow-up.
:::

:::summary
In one page: the reactivity series ranks metals by their reactions
with water and dilute acids (2.15) and by displacement reactions with
metal oxides and salt solutions (2.16); the order itself — K, Na, Li,
Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, (H), Cu, Ag, Au — is learnable and examinable
(2.17). Displacements are redox: oxidation is gain of oxygen/loss of
electrons, reduction is the reverse, and the oxidising agent is reduced
while the reducing agent is oxidised (2.20), with ionic equations and
half-equations as the bookkeeping. Iron rusts only with both oxygen
and water (2.18), and rusting is beaten by barrier methods,
galvanising or sacrificial protection (2.19). The listed practical
compares metals with dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids (2.21) —
and a valid comparison uses the same moles of metal, not the same
mass.
:::

:::can-you
- place an unfamiliar metal in the series from its reactions with water
  and dilute acids, stating the bracket each observation gives (spec
  2.15)?
- predict whether a metal displaces another from a metal oxide or a
  salt solution — and describe the observation, name the products and
  write the equation (spec 2.16)?
- recite the order K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, (H), Cu, Ag, Au and
  interpolate a new metal from its neighbours (spec 2.17)?
- state the two conditions iron needs to rust, and why salt accelerates
  it (spec 2.18)?
- compare barrier methods, galvanising and sacrificial protection —
  including why galvanised iron survives a scratch and tin plate does
  not (spec 2.19)?
- define oxidation, reduction, redox, oxidising agent and reducing
  agent in both oxygen and electron terms, and convert any displacement
  in this chapter into ionic and half-equations (spec 2.20)?
- outline the metals-with-dilute-acids practical, including why the
  same moles — not the same mass — of each metal makes the comparison
  valid (spec 2.21)?
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.18/2.19 items across the whole chapter. If
every line of the can-you checklist is a confident yes, Chapter 14 is
closed and you are carrying the full reactivity toolkit — the ranking,
the displacement rule, the redox vocabulary, the prediction method and
the rust-defence catalogue — into the papers.
:::
